subtype: Waiting until it is too late [Actor]
passage: The photocopy shop near the bus stand in Malerkotla was where the college seniors sat in the evenings. Three days before the cost accounting exam, Hafsa finally went there, her file clutched to her chest. She had missed most of October helping in her family's bangle shop during the wedding rush, and every week since, she had meant to catch up. Every week the pile looked more embarrassing. When classmates asked, she said, "Almost done revising." Nilesh, the senior who tutored, flipped through her half-empty notebook. "Hafsa, six chapters? In three days?" She stared at the floor. "I know." He was kind about it, but honest. "I can take you through two properly. Marginal costing and budgets carry the most marks. The rest you'll have to skim." Walking home past the closed shutters, she worked it out herself: back in early November, one hour a week would have been enough.

qa.q: How many chapters had Hafsa fallen behind on?
qa.a: Six chapters.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa wait until three days before the exam to ask?
qa.a: She felt ashamed as the pile grew, so she kept saying she was almost done revising instead of admitting she was behind.

qa.q: What could Hafsa have done in early November?
qa.a: She could have told Nilesh or a teacher right after the wedding rush that she had missed October, when an hour a week would have been enough.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel about only being able to cover two chapters?
qa.a: Nilesh is probably sorry and a little frustrated, wanting to help properly but knowing three days leave room for only the chapters with the most marks.

grounding: Shows a student who hides falling behind out of shame until the exam is close, which makes the gap bigger and the help harder to give.

passage:
Salma: hi Sangeeta, got 10 min today? one specific photo question, not a full lesson, promise 🙏
Sangeeta: haha go on
Salma: night shots of the fest stage keep coming out blurry
Salma: tried: tripod, 2-second timer, faster shutter
Salma: faster shutter fixes the blur but then they're dark and grainy
Salma: I'm stuck on what to change next. brightness vs grain is where I'm lost
Sangeeta: this is the nicest question anyone's sent me all week
Sangeeta: the dancers are moving, so a tripod won't save you. keep the fast shutter, open the aperture all the way, and accept a little grain
Sangeeta: grain looks like film. blur looks like a mistake
Salma: trying now
Salma: [photo]
Salma: SHARP. a bit grainy but sharp!!
Sangeeta: told you 🙂 come to the club meet on thursday and bring more

qa.q: What had Salma already tried before asking?
qa.a: A tripod, a 2-second timer and a faster shutter.

qa.q: Why did Salma add "not a full lesson, promise"?
qa.a: Salma was a little worried about imposing on Sangeeta's time and wanted to show respect by keeping the request small.

qa.q: Which parts of Salma's message made it easy to answer?
qa.a: Salma listed what had been tried, named the exact block, brightness versus grain, and asked for ten minutes, so Sangeeta could answer in a few lines.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta see Salma's question?
qa.a: Sangeeta is pleased and a bit impressed, calling it the nicest question all week, and even invites Salma to the club meet.

grounding: Illustrates asking for help after trying, naming exactly where the block is and what help is needed, which gets a quick and warm answer.

passage: I'm Naveen, and I've worked on the city desk of the paper for six years. When Wasim joined as a sub-editor, I noticed by Wednesday that he was retyping every headline by hand instead of using the saved styles. Each page took him an hour longer than it should. He stayed past ten three nights running. He never asked anyone anything. Whenever the desk chief walked by, he sat up straighter and scrolled, as if to look busy. I can't say what was going on in his head. He didn't seem lazy; if anything he was working twice as hard. My guess was that asking felt like admitting he didn't belong yet. On Thursday I pulled my chair over and said, "The style menu here is a nightmare. I was stuck on it for a week when I started." He let out a long breath. "Can you show me?"

qa.q: How was Wasim making the headlines instead of using the saved styles?
qa.a: Wasim was retyping every headline by hand.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while watching Wasim over those days?
qa.a: Naveen seems concerned and sympathetic, noticing the late nights and guessing that fear, not laziness, kept Wasim from asking.

qa.q: Why did Naveen's opening line work?
qa.a: Saying the menu is a nightmare and admitting to being stuck on it for a week made asking feel normal, so Wasim could ask without losing face.

qa.q: What is it like for Wasim when Naveen pulls a chair over?
qa.a: Wasim seems relieved, letting out a long breath, as if a weight lifted once someone else named the problem first.

grounding: Shows a senior noticing a new hire stuck for days and wasting effort, apparently out of fear of looking incompetent rather than laziness.

passage:

Jagdish: I got the Pune job. you moved there two years ago, right? could I ask how you found your flat and which areas work for the commute?
Kiran: congrats!!! 🎉
Kiran: in a review till 6 though. call at 7?
Jagdish: of course. sorry again, I know it's a lot to ask
Kiran: stop apologising 😄 honestly it made my day that you thought of me
[7:40 pm]
Jagdish: that was SO useful. I owe you. I felt bad taking 40 minutes
Kiran: I felt useful for the first time this week. my team only calls me when something's broken
Kiran: send me the listings you shortlist, I'll tell you which lanes flood in the monsoon
Jagdish: you're the best 🙏

qa.q: What time did Kiran suggest for the call?
qa.a: Kiran suggested a call at 7.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel about being asked for help?
qa.a: Kiran felt pleased and valued, saying it made the day and felt useful for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did Kiran do that kept the favour from becoming a burden?
qa.a: Kiran moved the call to after the review instead of answering mid-meeting, so the help came at a good time.

qa.q: How does Jagdish see the request compared with how Kiran sees it?
qa.a: Jagdish worries about imposing and apologises again and again, even after 40 minutes, while Kiran experiences it as trust rather than a burden.

grounding: Shows a person asked for advice who feels trusted and pleased rather than burdened, as long as the timing works, while the asker overestimates the imposition.

subtype: Sharing tasks in a student group [Actor]
passage: "Rehana, I've led a group twice this year and got it wrong both ways. I'm Irawati, by the way, for your listeners. First, the lake survey. I did the water samples, the photos, the report, even the bibliography. The others kept asking, 'What should we do?' and I kept saying, 'It's fine, I've got it.' By the end I was in tears over the printer, and Tushar told the professor he'd barely been allowed to help. He wasn't wrong. So for the street-play project I swung the other way. I sent one message: 'Script, props, posters, permissions. Pick one, bring it on the day.' No date to check in. Two people picked nothing and went quiet. The posters turned up on the morning of the show, spelled wrong. Next time I want one name next to each job, and one Friday where we all show what we've got."

qa.q: What did Irawati's message for the street-play project list?
qa.a: Script, props, posters and permissions: pick one, bring it on the day.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel at the end of the lake survey?
qa.a: Irawati was exhausted and overwhelmed, ending up in tears over the printer after doing every part alone.

qa.q: What went wrong both times, and what could fix it?
qa.a: First Irawati kept all the work, then handed it out with no check-in; clear owners for each job and one agreed checkpoint would fix both.

qa.q: How did Tushar see the lake survey?
qa.a: Tushar felt shut out and resentful, telling the professor he had barely been allowed to help.

grounding: Shows a student group leader who first takes on everything and then hands out pieces with no check-in, leading to resentment and members vanishing.

passage: In her first month as shift lead at the Andheri branch library, Ira had a habit. Avni would shelve the new arrivals, and after closing Ira would quietly re-shelve half of them. Avni would draft the poster for Saturday's story hour, and Ira would redo it at home because explaining the font rules took longer. "Faster if I just do it," she told herself, eating dinner at the desk at nine. By the fourth week, Ira was the only one who knew how to log inter-branch loans, set up the story-hour projector or file the monthly count. Then, one Saturday morning, her train was stuck for three hours. Twenty children and their parents waited in the reading room while Avni tried the projector cables one by one. When Ira arrived, Avni said quietly, "I didn't know how. You never let me."

qa.q: How long was Ira's train stuck on Saturday morning?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: Why did Ira keep redoing Avni's work?
qa.a: Ira felt uneasy trusting the work to someone else and told herself it was faster, so redoing it felt safer than explaining.

qa.q: What could Ira do differently from Monday?
qa.a: Ira could teach Avni the projector, the loan log and the monthly count one at a time and let Avni's poster stand, so the branch works without her.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about the way Ira has been working?
qa.a: Avni feels hurt and discouraged, left unable to help and then blamed in front of families, which comes out in "You never let me."

grounding: Shows a new lead who redoes tasks herself because it feels quicker, piling up her own workload while her colleague never learns.

passage: On Friday, Tanvir, manager of the Chembur cricket academy, messaged Darshan between two parent meetings: "Sort out the kit room before Monday." In Tanvir's head, that meant counting the helmets, setting aside the cracked ones, and listing what to order before the new batch of forty under-12s arrived. On Monday he opened the kit room door. It gleamed. Pads were stacked by size, bats hung on new hooks, the floor was mopped. There was no list. "Where's the count? What do we order?" Tanvir said, loud enough for the ground staff to hear. "You had all weekend." Darshan went red. "You said sort it out. I sorted it." Tanvir walked off muttering about people who don't think ahead. That night he scrolled back to his message. Seven words. He read it twice.

qa.q: How many under-12s were joining the academy?
qa.a: A new batch of forty under-12s.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have been feeling as he read his message twice that night?
qa.a: He was probably uneasy and a little embarrassed, starting to see that the gap was in his seven words, not in Darshan's effort.

qa.q: What could Tanvir have written on Friday instead?
qa.a: He could have said what the job was for and what he needed back: count the helmets, set aside cracked ones, and send a list of what to order before the new batch.

qa.q: How was the Monday exchange for Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan had worked hard all weekend and was then scolded in front of the ground staff, so it was humiliating and felt unfair.

grounding: Shows a manager who hands over a task in one vague line, is angry when the result differs from what he imagined, and blames the other person.

passage: At the community centre in Ludhiana, Gurleen stopped at Akash's desk on her way to a meeting. "Make something for Senior Citizens' Day, na? You'll manage." No date, no idea of what "something" meant. Akash, three weeks into the job, guessed. He spent two days designing a colourful quiz on old Punjabi film songs, printed thirty copies and laminated a sign. On Thursday Gurleen looked at it and frowned. "I needed the programme schedule for the notice board. And this print is too small for them to read. Didn't you think?" Akash said sorry and took the sheets back. That evening he stared at the unused quizzes, feeling foolish and set up. The next week, when she asked him to "fix the attendance sheet", he emailed her four questions before touching it and waited a whole day for her answers.

qa.q: How many copies of the quiz did Akash print?
qa.a: Thirty copies.

qa.q: How did Akash feel that evening, and why?
qa.a: He felt foolish and set up to fail, because he had guessed at a vague request in good faith and was then criticised for not reading Gurleen's mind.

qa.q: How could Gurleen hand over the next task more clearly?
qa.a: She could say what the thing is for, when it is due and what a good result looks like, for example a large-print programme schedule for the notice board by Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Akash's four-question email the next week?
qa.a: Gurleen may find it slow or fussy without realising her own vague request and sharp comment are what made him so cautious.

grounding: Shows a junior who guesses at a task given without context or standard, is criticised afterwards, and becomes much more cautious.

passage: "People ask why my team was so quiet last season. I'm Shreya, I run wedding events at a hotel in Udaipur, and the honest answer is: me. I gave Rehana the seating plan for a four-hundred-guest wedding and said, 'It's yours.' Then I messaged her every hour. Did you separate the two uncles who don't speak? Did you check the wheelchair spaces? At night I opened her file and moved tables around without telling her. I told myself it was about the client, that if one aunty ended up by the kitchen door, my name would be on it. By the third wedding, Rehana stopped suggesting anything. She'd say, 'Just tell me what you want, ma'am.' That sentence scared me more than any client. She wasn't lazy. She'd simply learned that her work wasn't really hers."

qa.q: How many guests were at the wedding whose seating plan Shreya handed to Rehana?
qa.a: Four hundred guests.

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel she had to check every hour?
qa.a: Shreya was anxious about being blamed if anything went wrong, believing her name would be on any mistake with the client.

qa.q: What could Shreya try with the next seating plan?
qa.a: Agree one or two check-in times with Rehana, ask questions instead of silently moving tables, and let Rehana's choices stand unless something is truly wrong.

qa.q: How did the hourly messages and silent changes look from Rehana's side?
qa.a: Rehana read them as distrust, so she felt discouraged and stopped offering ideas, waiting to be told what to do.

grounding: Shows a lead who hands off work but checks every step and rewrites it out of anxiety about accountability, so the team member stops taking ownership.

passage: The rain started at seven, an hour before sports day, and Rekha's phone buzzed: her brother said Ma's scan had moved to ten, and someone had to take her. Rekha found Disha in the staffroom, shaking out an umbrella. "I need to hand you the whole day," Rekha said. "Goal: every class finishes its events indoors by one. Why: lots of parents took half a day off to watch. Standard: equal turns for each house, first-aid table by the hall door, the little ones go first. How you arrange it is up to you. I'll ring at eleven. Tell me what's working and what isn't." Disha nodded, then began sketching on the back of a timetable. At eleven Rekha called from the hospital corridor. "Relays in the corridor, jumps in the hall," Disha said. "One question: tug-of-war?" "Skip it." By one, the last certificates had been handed out.

qa.q: By what time did every class need to finish its events?
qa.a: By one o'clock.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt handing over sports day at the last minute?
qa.a: Rekha was likely torn and anxious, needed by Ma and by the school at once, but steady enough to trust Disha with a clear plan.

qa.q: Which parts of Rekha's hand-over made it work?
qa.a: She gave the goal, the reason, the standard and a set check-in time, then left the method to Disha, so Disha could plan freely and still ask one question at eleven.

qa.q: What was the day like for Disha?
qa.a: Disha was probably nervous at first but felt trusted, sketched her own plan and ended up running the whole day confidently. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates delegating under pressure by giving the goal, the reason, the deadline and the standard, agreeing a check-in and leaving the method to the other person.
